ABSTRACT: Controlling the reaction selectivity to achieve a precision synthesis
is a constant concern for chemists. Here, we report a palladium-catalyzed
deaminative coupling of propargylamines with arylboronic acids to generate allene
skeletons. Importantly, this approach allows the regioselective γ-arylation of
unactivated propargyl tertiary amines to access various allenes in the absence of
amino-activating reagents. We present a wide range of propargylamines and
boronic acids and demonstrate the synthetic application of the target products to construct valuable compounds.
■ INTRODUCTION
The amine family, a wide range of building blocks, has been
extensively used as synthetic handles in synthetic chemistry
and medicinal chemistry.<sup>1</sup> Although amines ofer immense
synthetic leverage, the direct deaminative transformations of
tertiary amines remain underutilized because the amino group,
as a low heterolytic nucleofugal leaving group, has a high
homolytic C−N bond dissociation energy and stronger
characteristic basicity.<sup>2</sup> Accordingly, much efort has been
spent toward the deaminative functionalization of unactivated
tertiary amines. The classical method for C−N functionaliza-
tion involves the conversion of tertiary amines to ammonium
salts.<sup>3</sup> This preactivation strategy requires at least two distinct
transformations to achieve C−N functionalization. In addition,
in situ activation strategies such as the catalytic oxidation of
tertiary amines to form iminium intermediates<sup>4</sup> or the use of
activating agents<sup>5</sup> to induce deaminative functionalization have
been demonstrated. However, each of these previous reports
required the use of a large excess of oxidant or activator,
producing chemical waste that does not meet the demand for
green chemistry. Currently, many research groups have focused
on a variety of transition metal-catalyzed<sup>6</sup> and metal-free
strategies but are generally limited to aryl and benzylic tertiary
amines in cross-coupling reactions. To date, a few examples of
direct deaminative transformations of tertiary amines are stark
reminders of the shortcomings in this area of synthetic
chemistry. Therefore, developing a novel, eficient, and atom-
economic protocol for the C−N functionalization of tertiary
amines is highly important.
On the other hand, allenes have proven to be eficient and
versatile synthons in various cycloaddition reactions, providing
access to valuable molecules with medicinal, agrochemical, and
material significance.<sup>8</sup> They are also important scafolds widely
found in natural products, bioactive compounds, and marketed
drugs.<sup>9</sup> In this context, a great deal of eforts have been
devoted to the development of eficient approaches for the
construction of allene moieties.<sup>10</sup> In this regard, the transition
metal-catalyzed deaminative reaction has emerged as one of
the most attractive methods for the synthesis of allenes.<sup>11</sup>
Among these deaminative strategies, the C−N cleavage of
propargyl amines has been widely investigated, and various
metal catalysts such as Zn, Cu, In, Cd, Ag, Au, and Pd have
been employed (Scheme 1A).<sup>12</sup> However, these previous
reports mainly rely upon the use of specific substrates and limit
the structural diversity of allenes. The catalytic cross-coupling
of electrophilic propargyl derivatives with various nucleophiles
has ofered a promising approach for designing structural
diversity and complexity.<sup>13</sup> However, the reported deaminative
strategies to access allenes are limited to the utilization of
propargyl ammonium salts and organometallic reagents
through a process of γ-alkylation<sup>13b</sup> (Scheme 1B). To address
this shortfall, difluorocarbene-induced and alkyne-mediated
deaminative couplings of unactivated propargylamines and
boronic acids have been successfully developed by Song's
group<sup>14a</sup> and our group,
<sup>14b</sup> respectively, yielding propargylic
substitution products rather than allenes (Scheme 1C). The
exploitation of catalytic deaminative coupling methods to
access allenes using simple propargylamines and nucleophiles
remains underdeveloped, with the main challenge being
selective control to avoid the propargylic substitution reaction.
As part of our ongoing investigation into propargylamine
functionalizations, we report herein a novel palladium-
catalyzed deaminative coupling of propargyl tertiary amines
and arylboronic acids to construct diverse allenes via a
regioselective γ-arylation process (Scheme 1D).

■ CONCLUSIONS
In summary, a straightforward synthetic protocol has been
developed for the preparation of trisubstituted allenes via the
palladium-catalyzed deaminative coupling of unactivated
propargylamines and aryboronic acids. Importantly, we
demonstrate for the first time that this catalytic deaminative
coupling reaction can be achieved in the absence of any
external activator. Compared to the traditional catalytic
deaminative coupling via in situ amino activation, the
activator-free method ofers some sustainable features in
terms of operational simplicity, good functional group
tolerance with high yield and regioselectivity, and the absence
of toxic byproducts. Eforts to explore new synthetic
applications for activator-free catalytic deaminative trans-
formation are currently underway in our laboratory.
